source.title: Large Language Models Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts Across Typologically Diverse Languages
source.authors: Jannik Brinkmann; C. Wendler; Christian Bartelt; Aaron Mueller

record.tranche_reason: Tests for SAE-recoverable, cross-lingual grammatical features in Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B, extending representational evidence to these LLMs rather than reproducing the original toy-model experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper measures overlap among SAE features identified across languages and reports probe performance after feature ablations. Machine-translation steering results are not included as rows: they measure behavior after deliberate feature clamping, not whether that behavior arises naturally or the claimed representation geometry. The reported 13.9% (± 10.7%) cross-concept overlap is not assigned to a model because the text does not specify a model-level result.
record.test_reason: The study trains gated SAEs on Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B and uses their features as units to ask whether grammatical concepts are shared across languages. Its results are cross-language feature overlap (IoU among the top 32 features) and probe accuracy after ablating multilingual features. These measure multilinguality of the representation, not whether features are superposed, spread across neurons, or recoverable by a dictionary. SAE quality checks (loss recovered, qualitative interpretability) only validate the tool. None of V1–V6 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the authors conclude that both models, including the English-dominant Llama-3-8B, encode morphosyntactic concepts in feature directions shared across many languages. Ablating multilingual features pushes probes toward chance, and single-feature steering shifts translations selectively, though steering is imperfect.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains gated SAEs, uses probing classifiers and attribution patching to identify multilingual grammatical features, and tests ablations. It does not use the original toy-network superposition setup or its sparsity-and-importance geometry experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Probe and SAE activations are taken at layer 16; overlap is measured among the top 32 features; multilingual ablation includes features appearing in at least two languages, while the massively multilingual set is the upper quartile ranked by number of languages.

fits_no_version.finding: In Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B, top causal SAE features for grammatical concepts overlap across languages by up to ~50% IoU. Ablating multilingual features drops probe accuracy (Llama: 61% for all multilingual, 64% for top quartile).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features for morphosyntactic concepts in LLMs are shared across typologically diverse languages and are causally used by concept probes.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2025
record.problems: The representational evidence is limited to two 8B models and selected grammatical concepts and languages. Exact values for many figure results are not stated in the text. The paper notes that SAE recovery is limited to linearly encoded features, intrinsic interpretability lacks a ground-truth measure, and feature steering can require extreme activation values and produce degenerate outputs.
record.rows_left_out: Machine-translation steering efficacy and selectivity results in Figures 5-7 were left out because those outcomes follow deliberate feature clamping and do not measure naturally arising feature representations or their geometry.
record.verdict_notes: The SAE is used as a tool. The loss-recovered table (App. D.3, Llama-3-8B, 0.81–0.93 across nine mC4 languages) and the qualitative interpretability checks validate the dictionary rather than test V4. The paper explicitly says intrinsic interpretability can't be measured without ground truth. The limitations section notes SAEs recover only linear features and cites circular features, but runs no V6 test. Mean cross-concept overlap of 13.9% (±10.7%) is unassigned to a model and also bears on no version.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test superposition in toy networks, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry.
Does not test whether polysemanticity results from limited capacity, or whether important features obtain dedicated dimensions.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
Tests SAE-recoverable grammatical features in two models and selected languages; does not measure how broadly features are distributed across neurons in general.

Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units. It notes limitations of linear SAE recovery and that intrinsic interpretability cannot be measured without ground-truth features.
Does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional feature representations.

rows.subject: Llama-3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Measured cross-language intersection-over-union of the top 32 causally influential SAE features for each grammatical concept.

conditions.value: 23 selected UD languages; applicable languages vary by concept

rows.measure: Cross-language overlap of features associated with the same grammatical concept
rows.note: The text reports significant overlap, up to 50% across the models, but does not give exact model-by-concept values in text.
rows.check: Cross-language IoU of top-32 SAE features (Llama-3-8B) measures sharing across languages, not superposition or SAE recoverability; it does not bear on V4.

rows.subject: Llama-3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Identified a feature among the most influential for grammatical gender probes across languages.

conditions.value: 15 languages that inflect for grammatical gender

rows.measure: Number of languages in which the feature was among the most influential
rows.value: Feature 22860 was among the most influential across all 15 languages
rows.note: The paper describes the features as causally influential on the language-specific probe predictions.
rows.check: Feature 22860 is among the most influential gender features in all 15 gender-inflecting languages. This is an example of cross-lingual sharing, not evidence on V4.
